summary: Point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label switched paths may need paths computed before they are signaled. This document extends PCEP so a PCE can compute such paths, with one source and many destinations.

plainLanguage.summary:
Traffic engineering lets an operator ask for a specific route through a network rather than letting the routing protocol choose. For a path that fans out from one router to many, the path computation element had no way to answer.

This RFC adds that ability to the protocol a client uses to ask. One request can now name many destinations, say which of them are new and which are existing, and ask for the tree to be laid out so that the longest branch is as short as possible or the whole tree is as cheap as possible.

questions: how to compute p2mp lsp paths with pce
how does pce compute p2mp lsp paths
what are p2mp end-points leaf types
subtitle: Teaching the path computation protocol to work out paths for a one-to-many label-switched path.

tldr.problem: A path computation element can work out a path between two routers, but the protocol it speaks has no way to ask for a path from one router out to many. Point-to-multipoint traffic engineering paths need exactly that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends PCEP with new objects and flags: a flag in the request that says the request is for a one-to-many path, an end-points object that lists many destinations at once, two new objective functions for trees, and a branch-node object that says which routers may split the traffic.
tldr.outcome: A client can ask for a whole tree of paths in one request, add and remove destinations later, and reoptimize the existing tree. Destinations that cannot be reached are named in a separate object rather than left unexplained. The RFC obsoletes RFC 6006 and has since been updated by RFC 9353.

facts.label: Leaf types in a P2MP request

today: RFC 8306 is a Proposed Standard from November 2017. It obsoletes RFC 6006 and has since been updated by RFC 9353. The document also folds in five errata against the earlier specification and one against the base PCEP specification.

sections.title: Why the Protocol Needed a One-to-Many Extension
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element is an entity that can compute a network path or route based on a network graph and applying computational constraints. A Path Computation Client may make requests to a PCE for paths to be computed. The PCE has been identified as a suitable application for the computation of paths for point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label-switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

The PCE Communication Protocol is designed as a communication protocol between clients and elements for point-to-point path computations. However, that specification does not provide a mechanism to request path computation of point-to-multipoint paths.

A point-to-multipoint path is made of multiple source-to-leaf sub-paths. These are set up between ingress and egress label switching routers and are appropriately overlaid to construct the whole path. During path computation, the path may be determined as a set of source-to-leaf sub-paths computed separately and combined, or the whole tree may be determined in a single computation.

This document relies on the mechanisms of PCEP to request path computation for these paths. One request message may ask for the whole path to be computed, or the request may be limited to a subset of the sub-paths. In the extreme case the client may ask for the sub-paths to be computed individually, and it is the client's responsibility to decide whether to signal individual sub-paths or to combine the results to signal the whole path. The client may therefore use one request message or split the request across several.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-to-many path is a tree: one router at the top, splitting down to many routers at the leaves. The protocol for asking a planner for a path only knew how to ask for a single line between two points, so this RFC extends it to describe the whole tree.

sections.title: What the Extension Has to Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists the communication requirements the extension must satisfy, numbered as in the requirements document it comes from.

The client must be able to say that a request is for a point-to-multipoint path computation, and must be able to say that objective functions are to be applied to it. The PCE must have the capability to reject such a request and indicate that it does not support this kind of computation, and must provide an indication of non-support by implementations at an earlier level of the protocol.

A request must be able to list multiple destinations, and a response must be able to carry the path of a whole tree. By default the path returned by the PCE should use the compressed format. It must be possible for a single request or response to be conveyed by a sequence of messages.

Several requirements limit what the protocol may do. It must not be possible for a single request to specify a set of different constraints, traffic parameters or quality-of-service requirements for different destinations of the same tree, so all the branches of one request are treated alike. Path modification and path diversity must be supported, existing trees must be reoptimizable, and destinations must be addable and removable from existing paths.

The client must be able to specify a list of branch nodes to use when computing the path, must be able to discover whether the PCE supports this kind of computation at all, and must be able to request diverse paths when asking for a point-to-multipoint path.
sections.plainLanguage: One request covers one tree, and all the branches of that tree get the same constraints. Anything that needs different constraints per destination has to be split into separate requests.

sections.title: Discovering That a PCE Can Compute These Paths
sections.content:
Capability is advertised in two ways. The first is through the interior gateway protocol. The PCE Discovery TLV carried in an OSPF router information link state advertisement facilitates PCE discovery using OSPF, and that specification says no new sub-TLVs may be added to it. This document therefore defines a flag in the OSPF PCE capability flags to indicate the capability of point-to-multipoint computation. The same flag is used for the IS-IS sub-TLV so that IS-IS can indicate the same capability.

A PCE that supports the computation sets bit 10 accordingly. Clients that do not understand the bit ignore it, and PCEs that do not support it leave the bit clear. A PCE that sets the bit must then follow the procedures for the end-points object to further qualify the level of support it offers.

The second way is the Open message exchange. If a PCE does not advertise its capability during discovery, PCEP should be used so that a client can discover during the Open message exchange which PCEs can support the computation. To satisfy this, the Open object is extended with an optional type-length-value indicating the capability to perform point-to-multipoint computations. The value allocated from the PCEP TLV type indicator subregistry is 6, the description is P2MP capable, the length is 2 bytes and the value field is set to the default value of 0.

The inclusion of this element in an Open object indicates that the sender can perform point-to-multipoint path computations. The capability element is meaningful only for a PCE, so it will typically appear in only one of the two Open messages during session establishment. However, in the case of PCE cooperation, such as inter-domain operation, when a PCE behaving as a client initiates a session it should also indicate its path computation capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A router advertises in the routing protocol that it can plan these trees, and the client confirms it during the handshake. A client that meets an older planner gets a clean refusal rather than a confusing failure.

sections.title: The Objects That Carry the Request
sections.content:
The request parameters object is extended so that a client can signal a point-to-multipoint request, and the end-points object is extended to make the exchange more efficient. Three new flags are added to the request parameters object: to say that the request and reply have been fragmented across multiple messages, that they concern a point-to-multipoint path, and whether the route is represented in the compressed or uncompressed format.

Two new objects carry the route of an existing tree. The Secondary Explicit Route Object is used to specify the explicit route of a source-to-leaf sub-path, and has the same format as an explicit route object. The Secondary Record Route Object is used to record the explicit route of that sub-path. Both report the route of an existing path for which a reoptimization is desired. Their object class values are 29 and 30.

The end-points object is used in a request message to specify the source and destination addresses of the path to be computed. For a point-to-multipoint path, two types are defined: old leaves whose path can be modified or reoptimized, and old leaves whose path must be left unchanged. With the point-to-multipoint end-points object, one request message can list multiple destinations.

In total there are four possible types of leaf in a request: new leaves to add, old leaves to remove, old leaves whose path can be modified or reoptimized, and old leaves whose path must be left unchanged. Each end-points object gathers the leaves of one type, and the type is identified by a leaf type field in the object. Because the source address is repeated once rather than once per destination, the end-points portion of a request for many destinations can be reduced by up to 50% where a single source address has a very large number of destinations. A request can mix the types by including several end-points objects per request parameters object.

The body of the object for IPv4 starts with a leaf type field, then a source address and then the destination addresses. The body has a variable length: a multiple of 4 bytes for IPv4, and a multiple of 16 bytes plus 4 bytes for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The new end-points object lists the destinations once each, with a label saying whether each is new, being removed, or already there and free to move. Grouping them by label keeps the message small when there are thousands of destinations.

sections.title: Objective Functions and Metrics for a Tree
sections.content:
Six objective functions had been defined for point-to-point path computation. This document defines two more that apply to point-to-multipoint computation.

Objective function code 7 is Shortest-Path Tree, which minimizes the maximum source-to-leaf cost with respect to a specific metric, or the traffic engineering metric used as the default when no metric is specified. Objective function code 8 is Minimum-Cost Tree, which minimizes the total cost of the tree, that is the sum of the costs of the tree links, with respect to a specific metric or the same default.

Three metric types are added for the metric object, which already had three types for point-to-point computation. The new ones are the P2MP IGP metric with value 8, the P2MP traffic engineering metric with value 9, and the P2MP hop count metric with value 10. These encode the sum of the metrics of all the links of the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of shaping the tree are offered. One makes the worst branch as short as possible. The other makes the whole tree as cheap as possible, counting every shared link once.

sections.title: Adding and Removing Destinations
sections.content:
When adding new leaves to or removing old leaves from an existing tree, the client supplies a list of the existing leaves, and the tree can be optimized as a result.

To add new leaves the client must build a request using end-points with leaf type 1. To remove old leaves it must build a request using end-points with leaf type 2. If no type 2 end-points exist, the PCE must send an error of type 17 with value 1, meaning that it cannot satisfy the request because there are no end-points of leaf type 2.

When adding or removing leaves the client must also provide the list of old leaves, if any, using end-points of leaf type 3, leaf type 4, or both. Specific error objects and types are used when these conditions are not met, and a generic inconsistent end-points error is used when a request is inconsistent, for example when a leaf specified as type 1 already exists.

For old leaves the client must provide the old path as a list of record route objects that immediately follows each end-points object.

Two further mechanisms round out the protocol. Before computing the path, a PCE may need to know which nodes in the network are capable of acting as branch routers, and it can discover that with the mechanisms of the PCE discovery document. The client can specify a list of nodes that may be used as branch nodes, or a list that may not, using the Branch Node Capability object, which has the same format as the include route object except that it supports only IPv4 and IPv6 prefix sub-objects. A request may carry at most one such object.

Large requests are split. The total PCEP message length, including the common header, is 16 bytes, and a tree with many hundreds or thousands of leaves may not fit into one message. The fragmentation bit in the request parameters object signals that the request or response was too large to fit in one message, and every message of the series carries the same request or response identifier so that the pieces can be told apart. The assumption is that the messages are reliably delivered and in sequence, since PCEP relies on TCP.

Finally, a request may fail because all or some of the destinations are unreachable, and the UNREACH-DESTINATION object lets the PCE name the unreachable destinations. It can be present in reply messages, and there can be up to one such object per request parameters object. Its object class is 28, with object type 1 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Destinations can be added and dropped later, and the tree can be reshaped when that happens. If some destinations cannot be reached, the planner names them rather than silently leaving them out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Point-to-multipoint path computation requests are more CPU-intensive and use more link bandwidth than point-to-point ones. In the event of an unauthorized request or a denial-of-service attack, the resulting requests and processing may be disruptive to the network, so implementations should follow the security requirements that help to minimize or negate unauthorized requests and denial-of-service attacks.

Securing the PCEP session requests and responses is recommended using TCP security techniques such as the TCP Authentication Option or Transport Layer Security, following the recommendations and best current practices of the transport security document. Authenticating the requests and responses, so that the message is intact and came from an authorized node, is recommended using the same mechanisms. Policy control could be provided by explicitly defining which clients are allowed to send point-to-multipoint requests, using IP access lists.

Because PCEP operates over TCP, it is also important to secure the PCE and the client against TCP denial-of-service attacks. Implementations should support the TCP Authentication Option and not use TCP MD5, because of that algorithm's known vulnerabilities and weakness.
sections.plainLanguage: These requests are expensive to compute, so an attacker who can send them freely could hurt the network. The recommendation is to run the session over an authenticated and encrypted transport, and to use access lists to decide who may ask.

viz.caption: What the protocol can do to an existing tree

items.title: Add destinations
items.text: A request with leaf type 1 asks for new leaves, and the existing tree can be optimized as a result.

items.title: Remove destinations
items.text: A request with leaf type 2 removes old leaves.

items.title: Reoptimize
items.text: The client sends the old routes so the planner can lay the tree out again.

items.title: Name what cannot be reached
items.text: The unreachable destinations are listed in their own object in the reply.

items.title: Costly requests
items.text: A one-to-many computation uses more processor time and more link bandwidth than a one-to-one one, so an unauthorized request or a denial-of-service attack can be disruptive.

items.title: Protect the session
items.text: Securing the session with the TCP Authentication Option or TLS is recommended, and requests and responses should be authenticated so the message is intact and comes from an authorized node.

items.title: Policy control
items.text: Access lists can define which clients are allowed to send these requests.

items.title: TCP resilience
items.text: Because the protocol runs over TCP, the planner and the client must also be protected against TCP denial-of-service attacks.
